To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the number of patients in clinical trials of new radiotherapy protocols must be large, and that the trials must be stratified to ensure that the patients have the same risk for local recurrence.

the steepness of tumor dose-response curve, the steepness of normal tissue tolerance dose-response curve, and the number of patients to be treated in the control arm, are all important factors in the calculation of the number of patients required in a clinical trial.

(1) the steepness of a dose-response curve is a key factor determining the size of a clinical trial; (2) a trial of dose escalation should be designed with the aim of obtaining the maximum information about the dose-response curve; and (3) the design of a trial of dose-fractionation should be based on a detailed analysis of the dose-response curves for the tumor and the normal tissue.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: What are the dose-response relationships for both tumor and normal tissue, for different types of treatment?

the design and analysis of clinical trials in radiotherapy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the size of a clinical trial should be based on a detailed analysis of the specific problem, including a careful review of the literature, a detailed analysis of all the relevant data, and a careful consideration of the possible uncertainties in the data and in the assumptions.

a trial with a biologically motivated rationale should be designed with the following features: a large number of patients (at least 300), stratification of patients according to the risk of a specific type of recurrence, and a detailed description of the patient population, including the results of predictive assays.

a trial of a new treatment should be designed in such a way that it will be possible to answer a clinically relevant question, and the number of patients required should not exceed the maximum number of patients that can be included in the trial.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
it is possible to calculate with some confidence how large a clinical trial should be to answer a given question, but it is difficult to predict how large the effect of a new treatment will be.
the radiobiological basis for the design of a clinical trial is a necessary but not sufficient condition to justify the size of the trial.
the number of patients required in a randomized clinical trial is inversely related to the steepness of both the tumor and normal tissue response curves.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the design of clinical trial should be based on a radiobiological model.

it is important for the clinical researcher to have some knowledge of the radiobiological rationale behind the design of the trial, in order to be able to assess the size of the trial required to achieve a given level of statistical significance.
it is possible to design a clinical trial that has a high probability of success.
